explanations.answer: They won't see his face again without their brother
explanations.explanation: Judah, one of Jacob's sons, tells his father the man said, "You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you." That's the whole deal, plain as day. No brother, no meeting. I think the brothers felt that sentence in their stomachs the whole way home.

explanations.answer: They won't get more grain unless they pay double
explanations.explanation: Close to the money talk, but the man's warning wasn't about the price. Judah says it was about seeing his face again without their brother. The double silver comes up later, and it's Israel's idea, not the man's (Genesis 43:12). Israel is Jacob's other name, by the way.

explanations.answer: They won't leave Egypt alive a second time
explanations.explanation: That would be some dramatic warning, but it isn't in the text. Judah says the man warned them, "You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you." It's about the face and the brother. Nothing in it says anything about the brothers leaving or not leaving alive.

Judah actually says the opposite. He says that if their father sends the brother, "we will go down and buy food for you." But if not, "we will not go." So the trip depends on the brother coming. Judah has a very clear policy here.

Right, Judah gives his father two options. Send their brother, and they'll go down and buy food. Don't send him, and he says, "we will not go." He says it twice, the second time with the man's warning right behind it. That's a man who wants to be heard.

explanations.answer: Telling the man they had another brother
explanations.explanation: Israel asks, "Why did you tell the man you had another brother?" He's looking at what was said in Egypt. The brothers answer that the man questioned them in detail about their family, and they just answered him. I think nobody at that table was enjoying this conversation.

explanations.answer: Coming home with too little grain
explanations.explanation: Israel doesn't blame them for that. He is the one who tells them to go back and buy a little more food, because they've eaten all the grain they brought. His complaint is about something they told the man: "Why did you tell the man you had another brother?"

explanations.answer: Bowing down to the man in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Bowing doesn't come up in his question at all. Israel asks, "Why did you bring this trouble upon me?" and then points to one thing they said. That was telling the man they had another brother. Keep your eyes on that line.

Judah says, "I will guarantee his safety. You may hold me personally responsible." Then he adds that if he doesn't bring Benjamin back and set him before his father, he'll bear the guilt all his life. Judah puts himself on the line. No extra helpers, no fine print.

explanations.answer: He'll give his own two sons as a pledge
explanations.explanation: That was Reuben's offer, another of Jacob's sons, back when the first trip went sideways. He told his father, "You may put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you" (Genesis 42:37). Judah's offer this time is different. He puts himself on the line: "You may hold me personally responsible."

explanations.answer: He'll hire guards to watch over Benjamin
explanations.explanation: No guards in this story. Judah doesn't bring in anyone else. He says, "I will guarantee his safety," and tells his father to hold him personally responsible. The promise is his own.

Judah says, "If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now." He's pointing out that all this waiting has cost them. It's like the friend who tells you the shortcut after you've already driven the long way. He's not wrong, though.

Actually, it's right there in the text. Judah says, "If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now." The waiting has cost them time. I think he's trying to get his father to see that.

Israel's list is "a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachios and almonds." So honey, almonds and myrrh are all in the pack. These are some of the best products of the land, packed up as a gift for the man. Somebody was packing with care.

explanations.answer: Wine and figs and olive oil
explanations.explanation: That's a nice basket, but it isn't Israel's. His list is "a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachios and almonds." No wine, no figs, no olive oil. The gift is honey and the rest of that list.
None of those make the list. Israel says to carry down "a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachios and almonds." That's the gift for the man. Wool, barley and dates stay home.

Israel says, "Take double the silver with you so that you may return the silver that was put back into the mouths of your sacks." So they bring the first silver back and more to buy food. Then he adds, "Perhaps it was a mistake." That's a father covering every angle.
Half would leave them short. Israel says the opposite: "Take double the silver with you." That covers the silver put back in their sacks, and he says perhaps it was a mistake. More silver, not less.

Triple is a lot of silver, and Israel doesn't ask for it. He says, "Take double the silver with you so that you may return the silver that was put back into the mouths of your sacks." Double is the number.

Israel says it just as written: "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, that he may release your other brother along with Benjamin." He's asking God for mercy for his sons. The other brother is the one kept back in Egypt (Genesis 42:24). Sending them off with that sentence is a father doing what he can.

It's in the text, word for word. Israel says, "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, that he may release your other brother along with Benjamin." The brother kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24) is on his mind. So is Benjamin.

explanations.answer: He's ready to accept losing his sons
explanations.explanation: Israel says, "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." I think he's bracing himself for the worst. He prays for mercy first, then lets them go. That's not an easy thing for a father to say out loud.

explanations.answer: He's sure the man will send them back
explanations.explanation: Israel isn't sure of anything. He says, "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man." That's a prayer for something he hopes for. Then he says, "if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." Nobody says that when they're certain.

explanations.answer: He's planning to go down to Egypt himself
explanations.explanation: Israel stays home in this passage. He sends his sons with the gifts, the double silver and Benjamin. Then he says, "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." That's a man waiting at home.

explanations.answer: Take them to his house and prepare a meal
explanations.explanation: Joseph, the man in charge in Egypt, tells his steward, "Take these men to my house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, for they shall dine with me at noon." It's a dinner order. The brothers don't know it yet, and they're about to get nervous over it.

explanations.answer: Lock them up for three days
explanations.explanation: Joseph did put his brothers in custody for three days on their first visit (Genesis 42:17). This time his order is a meal: "Take these men to my house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, for they shall dine with me at noon." Same man, very different order.

explanations.answer: Send them straight back to Canaan
explanations.explanation: That isn't his order. Joseph sees Benjamin with them and tells the steward to take them to his house and prepare a meal, "for they shall dine with me at noon." Nobody is being sent anywhere before lunch.

The brothers say it themselves: "They intend to overpower us and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys." They link it to the silver found in their bags the first time. Donkeys included. Nobody's getting left out of this plot in their heads.

The text says they really do fear this. They say, "We have been brought here because of the silver that was returned in our bags the first time." Then: "They intend to overpower us and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys." That's a long list of worries before lunch.

The steward says, "Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks. I received your silver." He tells them not to be afraid. That's a calm answer for men who came in braced for the worst.

explanations.answer: A servant who made a mistake
explanations.explanation: The steward doesn't blame a servant. He says, "Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks." He also says, "I received your silver." His answer points to God, not a mix-up.
Pharaoh doesn't come up in the steward's answer. He says, "Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks." Then he adds that he received their silver.

The steward brings Simeon out to them. He's the brother who was kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24). The steward says it's fine, and then Simeon walks out. I think that's about the best way to hear "do not be afraid."
Reuben is another of Jacob's sons, but he's not the one the steward brings out. The text says the steward "brought Simeon out to them." Simeon is the brother who was kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).
Levi is another of Jacob's sons, but the text names Simeon here. The steward "brought Simeon out to them." Simeon was the brother kept in Egypt (Genesis 42:24).

explanations.answer: Bow to the ground before him
explanations.explanation: The text says it right after the gifts: "they presented him with the gifts they had brought, and they bowed to the ground before him." Joseph is the man they've been so nervous about. They come in humbly.

explanations.answer: Ask him to sell them grain
explanations.explanation: That's why they came to Egypt, but it's not what happens here. After the gifts, "they bowed to the ground before him." The grain isn't what they're doing in this moment.
No travel stories at this point. The text says they presented the gifts and "bowed to the ground before him." After that, Joseph is the one asking the questions.
They say the opposite. Joseph asks about their father, and they answer, "Your servant our father is well. He is still alive." Then they bow down to honor him. Good news, delivered with a bow.
They tell Joseph, "Your servant our father is well. He is still alive." Joseph had just asked, "Is he still alive?" So the answer is yes, and they bow down to honor him after saying it.
The text says Joseph "was moved to tears for his brother" and went to a private room to weep. I think seeing Benjamin hit him hard. It's a tender moment, so let it be tender.
The text says something softer. Joseph hurried out "because he was moved to tears for his brother." Then he went to a private room to weep.
No laughing here. The text says Joseph "was moved to tears for his brother, and he went to a private room to weep." This is a tender moment, and I'll keep my jokes out of it.

explanations.answer: Eating with Hebrews was detestable to them
explanations.explanation: The text says, "the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them." So the meals were served separately, one for Joseph, one for his brothers and one for the Egyptians. Three tables, one house.

explanations.answer: The brothers were still under arrest
explanations.explanation: They're guests at Joseph's house, not prisoners. The steward told them not to be afraid and gave them water to wash their feet. The text gives a different reason for the separate meals: eating with Hebrews "was detestable to them."

explanations.answer: There wasn't room for everyone together
explanations.explanation: Space isn't the reason the text gives. It says, "the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them." So Joseph, his brothers and the Egyptians were served separately.
The text says they were seated in order by age, "and the men looked at one another in astonishment." It doesn't say why. I'd be staring at my brothers too if the seating chart knew my birth order.

The text says it: they were seated "in order by age, from the firstborn to the youngest, and the men looked at one another in astonishment." It doesn't tell us why they were astonished. They sure noticed, though.

explanations.answer: Five times larger than any other
explanations.explanation: The text says, "Benjamin's portion was five times larger than any of the others." Five times, friend. That's five cookies on his plate for every one on theirs. Then they all feasted and drank freely with Joseph.

explanations.answer: Exactly the same as the others
explanations.explanation: Not even close. The text says, "Benjamin's portion was five times larger than any of the others." That's a lot of food. Somebody at that table got the big plate.

explanations.answer: Half the size of the others
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. Benjamin's portion "was five times larger than any of the others." Nobody was passing him the small plate. He got the biggest one by far.
